medium.titulo: Do Chess Masters Really Think More Moves Ahead?
medium.autor: Johnny Y. Lewis from Strcutured Thinking Lab
medium.resumo: How many moves ahead can a chess master see?
medium.conteudo_html:
https://medium.com/media/c48bcee8ea1e04c9ca4371ecb12449a6/href

How many moves ahead can a chess master see?

It sounds like a simple question.

A chess position may offer dozens of legal moves. Each of those moves leads to several possible replies, which lead to several more replies after that.

Very quickly, the number of possible paths becomes enormous.

So the obvious explanation for chess expertise seems to be this:

The better the player, the more possibilities they can calculate — and the farther ahead they can see.

But that is not quite how expertise works.

Experts Don’t Search Everything

Classic research by psychologist Adriaan de Groot examined how strong chess players think about positions.

One of the most interesting findings was that elite players were not simply calculating vastly more moves than weaker players.

Their advantage appeared earlier in the process.

They were better at identifying which moves were worth analyzing in the first place.

A novice may look at a position and consciously examine many different possibilities.

An expert, by contrast, recognizes familiar patterns.

Certain moves immediately look promising. Others can be dismissed quickly.

That means the expert does not need to explore every branch of the decision tree.

They can narrow the search space before doing the deeper calculation.

In simplified form:

Novice:
“Here are ten possible moves. Let me examine all of them.”

Expert:
“These three moves matter. Let me examine them carefully.”

Expertise, then, may be less about searching more and more about knowing where to search.

More Options Are Not Always Better

This idea extends far beyond chess.

We usually assume that having more options is good.

If a store offers 30 laptops instead of three, there is a greater chance that one of them perfectly matches what we need.

If an investor considers more assets, there may be more opportunities.

If a researcher generates more hypotheses, one of them may turn out to be right.

If a doctor considers more possible diagnoses, an unusual disease may be less likely to be overlooked.

More options increase the chance that a better answer is somewhere in the set.

But they also create another problem.

Every additional option must be understood, compared, evaluated, and eventually accepted or rejected.

So expanding the choice set does two things at once:

It increases the chance of finding a better answer.

But it also:

increases the cost of finding that answer.

Chess masters become powerful partly because they reduce that second cost.

They learn which branches of the tree are worth exploring.

Maybe Expertise Is Really About Attention

This changes the way we think about expertise.

An expert may not simply be someone who knows more or thinks harder.

An expert may be someone who knows:

what deserves attention — and what does not.

That distinction matters.

When a beginner faces a complicated problem, many possibilities can appear equally important.

An expert sees structure.

Some possibilities become more salient. Others disappear almost immediately.

The expert is not necessarily processing everything.

They are allocating their limited attention more effectively.

You could summarize the difference as:

Not More Search. Better Search.

AI Makes This Problem Even More Important

Generative AI makes this idea especially relevant.

Until recently, generating possibilities was often expensive.

Coming up with 20 business ideas took time.

Developing ten explanations for an economic phenomenon required effort.

Producing multiple versions of an article, investment thesis, research question, or marketing concept could take hours.

Now we can ask an AI:

“Give me 20 alternatives.”

And seconds later, we have them.

The cost of generating options is collapsing.

But the cost of evaluating options has not disappeared.

AI can generate 20 business ideas in seconds, but determining which one has a viable market may take weeks.

It can generate ten explanations for an economic event, but figuring out which explanation is consistent with the evidence still requires judgment.

It can produce dozens of strategies, but someone still has to decide which ones are worth testing.

This creates an interesting reversal.

When ideas were scarce, generating more ideas was valuable.

When ideas become nearly unlimited, the scarce resource may become something else:

the ability to discard them.

The more easily we can generate possibilities, the more valuable it becomes to know which possibilities deserve our attention.

The Hidden Structure

Chess may look like a very specialized activity.

But the underlying problem is surprisingly general.

We face the same structure whenever the number of possible actions becomes larger than our ability to evaluate them.

Chess players face it when choosing moves.

Doctors face it when considering diagnoses.

Investors face it when comparing opportunities.

Researchers face it when selecting hypotheses.

And increasingly, all of us face it when using AI.

The important question may no longer be:

How many possibilities can we generate?

It may be:

How quickly can we identify the few possibilities that are actually worth thinking about?

That is the hidden structure behind this episode of Hidden Structure.

The video starts with chess, but moves into a much broader question:

Can having more choices actually make our decisions worse?

Watch the video to see how the same pattern appears across decision-making, medicine, investing, and AI.

medium.titulo: We Simulated Natural Selection in Game Theory AI. The Extinction Cycle Shocked Us.
medium.resumo: What happens when algorithms reproduce based on their wealth and starve when they fail? The tragedy of naive kindness, the invasion of…
medium.conteudo_html:
What happens when algorithms reproduce based on their wealth and starve when they fail? The tragedy of naive kindness, the invasion of trust, and the mathematics of evolutionary survival.

In our previous experiments, we treated game theory like an academic seminar.

We invited an eclectic mix of synthetic personalities into our laboratory: pure altruists who always cooperate, ruthless predators who always defect, and reciprocal enforcers like Tit-for-Tat who mirror whatever you do. We let them play thousands of rounds, tallied up their scores, and crowned our winners on a digital leader-board.

It was comforting to see that nice algorithms generally finished at the top.

But we were playing god.

In our laboratory, no agent ever had to worry about rent. No algorithm ever starved. If a strategy scored terribly, it remained in the society round after round, protected by our experimental script.

In the real world, nature has no tenure.

In biological ecosystems, organisms that fail to secure calories go extinct. In economic markets, companies that burn cash without profit go bankrupt. In social networks and corporate cultures, toxic behaviors drive healthy members away, while extractive habits spread if left unchecked.

So we decided to remove the safety net.

We introduced Replicator Dynamics to The Dilemma Experiment: Every generation, agents play a full tournament. Strategies that earn above-average fitness multiply and expand their offspring. Strategies that earn below-average fitness contract — and if their numbers hit zero, they are permanently extinct.

Here is what happened when our artificial society had to survive on its own merits.

Act I: The Feast of the Predators (The Altruist-Predator Collapse)

To see natural selection in its rawest, most brutal form, we created a digital garden with 100 inhabitants:

  • 50 Altruists (AlwaysCooperate): Unconditional saints who always extend a hand.
  • 50 Predators (AlwaysDefect): Ruthless opportunists who betray every single time.
Generation 0: 50 Altruists  |  50 Predators

In Generation 0, the predators thought they had discovered paradise.

Every time a predator encountered an altruist, it pocketed the maximum sucker payoff: +5+5 points, while the altruist absorbed a painful 00. The predators feasted. Their average score reached an astronomical 3,4503,450 points per agent. The altruists scraped by with just 1,0101,010 points.

When the reproduction cycle kicked in, the mathematics were merciless:

Gen 0: [██████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Altruist (50%) | [██████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Predator (50%)
Gen 1: [█████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Altruist (33%) | [███████████████████░░░░░░░░░] Predator (67%)
Gen 2: [█████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Altruist (17%) | [███████████████████████░░░░░] Predator (83%)
Gen 3: [██░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Altruist ( 6%) | [██████████████████████████░░] Predator (94%)
Gen 4: [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Altruist ( 1%) | [████████████████████████████] Predator (99%)
Gen 5: [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Altruist ( 0%) | [████████████████████████████] Predator (100%)

In just five generations, the altruists collapsed from 50 to 33, then 17, then 6, then 1, and then total extinction.

The Starvation of the Victorious

The predators had won. They owned 100% of the digital earth.

And that was their undoing.

With the last altruist dead, there was no one left to exploit. Every predator was now forced to face another predator. When two predators meet, both defect: mutual defection yields a pathetic +1+1 point per round.

Look at what happened to the wealth of the civilization:

  • At the peak of the feast, population mean fitness was 2,230.0 points per agent.
  • In their all-predator utopia, mean fitness collapsed to 990.0 points per agent.

The society suffered a 55.6% destruction of total social wealth.

The Lesson for Human Systems: Unconditional altruism feeds toxic parasites. But pure selfishness is ecologically suicidal: it multiplies until it consumes its host, then starves in the wasteland it created.

Act II: The Invasion Barrier (Can Trust Conquer a Corrupt World?)

Now we posed the inverse question: Suppose a civilization has completely fallen to cynical self-interest. Everyone defects. Everyone expects betrayal.

Can trust ever return?

We dropped 2 Tit-for-Tat agents into a population of 98 Predators.

Initial Roster: 2 Reciprocal Agents  vs  98 Predators

Tit-for-Tat is not a naive doormat: it starts with cooperation, but retaliates instantly if you betray it.

Yet when dropped into a 98% predator population, the 2 good guys were obliterated:

  • Each Tit-for-Tat agent had to play 98 predators and only 1 fellow cooperator.
  • On Round 1 against each predator, Tit-for-Tat extended a hand and got burned (00 points vs +5+5). Even though it defected for the remaining rounds, that initial loss was fatal.
  • The 2 Tit-for-Tat agents scored 912912 points on average.
  • The 98 predators scored 998998 points on average.

Because their fitness was lower, the isolated good guys went extinct.

A lone cooperator in a corrupt neighborhood cannot survive on ideals alone.

Act III: The Power of the Cluster

Then, we ran the experiment again. But this time, we changed one variable: clustering.

Instead of 2 agents, we introduced 20 Tit-for-Tat agents into 80 Predators.

Initial Roster: 20 Reciprocal Agents  vs  80 Predators

Look at the difference: With 20 agents, each cooperator now interacts with 19 fellow cooperators!

In those matches, they don’t fight: they cooperate for all 10 rounds, reaping +3/+3+3/+3 on every single exchange (3030 points per match).

That mutual cooperative dividend was enough to tip the mathematical scale:

  • The 20 Tit-for-Tat agents earned an average of 1,290 points.
  • The 80 Predators earned an average of 1,070 points.

The evolutionary takeover was breathtaking:

Gen 00: [██████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] TFT (20%) | [████████████████████████░░░░] Predator (80%)
Gen 02: [████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] TFT (27%) | [██████████████████████░░░░░░] Predator (73%)
Gen 04: [████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] TFT (41%) | [██████████████████░░░░░░░░░░] Predator (59%)
Gen 06: [███████████████████░░░░░░░░░] TFT (63%) | [███████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Predator (37%)
Gen 08: [█████████████████████████░░░] TFT (85%) | [█████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Predator (15%)
Gen 10: [████████████████████████████] TFT (96%) | [█░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Predator ( 4%)
Gen 12: [████████████████████████████] TFT (99%) | [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Predator ( 1%)
Gen 13: [████████████████████████████] TFT (100%)| [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] Predator ( 0%)
        ⚡ TOTAL CONQUEST: Always Defect driven to 0% EXTINCTION!

In 13 generations, the 20% minority completely eradicated the 80% predator majority!

As evolutionary biologist W.D. Hamilton and political scientist Robert Axelrod proved in 1981:

“A world of pure defectors can resist invasion by isolated individuals, but cannot resist invasion by a cluster of cooperators.”

If you want to change a toxic culture, you don’t send one martyr into the fray. You build a tight, aligned cluster that protects each other until the compounding returns of cooperation conquer the room.

Act IV: The Noise Crucible (The Survival of the Forgiving)

Finally, we threw all 8 archetypes into a realistic evolutionary arena under 5% communication noise.

In a noisy world, hands tremble: emails are misread, network packets drop, and innocent comments sound hostile.

Under these conditions, who survives?

Gen 25 Demographics under 5% Noise:
  Grim Trigger (Legalist)     [████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] 28.6%
  Tit-for-Tat (Reciprocator)  [█████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] 17.3%
  Tit-for-Two-Tats (Patient)  [████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] 14.3%
  Generous TFT (Forgiving)    [████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] 13.3%
  Pavlov (Adaptive)           [███░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] 12.2%
  Always Cooperate (Altruist) [██░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░]  8.2%
  Always Defect (Predator)    [█░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░]  3.1%
  Random (Chaos)              [█░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░]  3.1%

The findings were profound:

  1. Predators and Chaos collapsed: Selfish opportunists dropped from 25%25% of the world to just 6%6%. As the society wised up, exploiters were starved of victims.
  2. Retaliation is an Ecological Shield: Strategies with teeth (GrimTrigger, TitForTat) acted as an immune system, ruthlessly punishing defectors.
  3. Forgiveness is an Evolutionarily Stable Strategy (ESS): In an imperfect world, patient and forgiving strategies (TitForTwoTats, GenerousTitForTat, Pavlov) survived without bleeding points in retaliatory vendettas.

The Three Laws of Evolutionary Resilience

If our digital simulation teaches us anything about engineering, leadership, and human society, it is this:

  1. Never be a doormat: Unconditional kindness without boundaries invites predation and creates demographic collapse.
  2. Find your cluster: Real change begins with a small, cohesive group practicing mutual reciprocity.
  3. Forgive the noise: In any complex system, misunderstandings will happen. Brittle systems break. Resilient systems forgive.

The Dilemma Experiment is an open-source research initiative exploring cooperation and emergent behavior in multi-agent systems.

Explore the full technical documentation, mathematical proofs, and code on GitHub: synthex-labs-hq/the-dilemma-experiment.

medium.titulo: Ask for the blast radius before the edit.
medium.resumo: An open file is not a map. Callers you never loaded are where the break lands.
medium.conteudo_html:
An open file is not a map. Callers you never loaded are where the break lands.

I used to trust a change because the file looked right on the screen. The agent had read it. The diff was tidy. The tests on that path were green. Then something three hops away broke, in a flow nobody opened that afternoon.

The edit was locally sensible. That is exactly why it was dangerous.

An open file is not a map.

I keep seeing the same freeze when teams turn coding agents on.

Managers feel surprise first. A refactor that used to take a week lands before lunch. Then confusion. Which callers moved. Which flows still run. Then a quiet desperation. I used to feel in control when I could point at a person who knew the call chains by heart. Now the draft arrives faster than the room can name what depends on what, and the old review calendar no longer maps to the risk.

Old-school developers feel it from the other side. They can still smell a bad change. They also watch a model rewrite a helper inside systems they spent years protecting. When the answer is “the agent had the file open,” craft has nowhere to stand. So they lean into the transcript. They try to police every tool call. They call that control.

It is not control. It is a flashlight pointed at one building while the roads stay dark.

Engineering was always cumbersome. Specs. Guardrails. Tests. Reviews that ask which callers break. The boring parts that kept a Friday from becoming an incident. AI did not invent that grind. It removed the waiting that used to hide risk behind calendar time.

My take, not a study: if you keep a real spec, real guardrails, and real tests, AI can produce the same quality of work about ten times faster. The ten times is the speed of getting to something you can actually ship. It is not a license to edit without a picture of the blast radius.

Speed without that picture just moves the loss of control into a confident green checkbox on the wrong surface.

That is why I treat architectural awareness as part of the harness, not as a nice diagram on a wiki.

In our own delivery on Digilist and Bevillingsportal, the pattern shows up the same way it does in older fagsystemer. A change that looks clean in one module can drag quiet dependencies with it: a report someone still runs by hand, a file drop into accounting, a shared component nobody documented because it had worked for years. The Norwegian version of the modernization habit is on the Xala blog: change the system module by module, with full operation, because you know what hangs off each piece before you cut it. https://xala.no/blogg/modernisere-fagsystem-uten-driftsstans

Agents make the same mistake humans make when they modernize without a map. They optimize the page they can see. They miss the callers they never loaded.

So what do I ask for before I let an agent touch a live path.

I ask for three lines that fit on a card:

target     what symbol or module will change
callers    who calls it, and which flows those calls sit in
confidence how sure we are the list is complete

Those three lines are boring on purpose. Boring is how trust survives speed.

Then I change the order of work.

ask blast radius before the edit
prefer read paths before write paths
keep the dependency map fresh on every commit
do not ship a locally green change with unknown callers

A stale map is worse than none. It teaches the room to trust a picture that is already wrong. If you cannot refresh the index when the code moves, do not pretend the map is a gate. Put the gate somewhere else: a test that covers the flow, a review that names the callers, a human who may still say no.

The org also needs one shared picture of the system. Not twelve private chats where each agent got a different slice of context. Not a hero who still holds the call chains in their head. If only one person can answer “what breaks if we change this,” you do not have control. You have a single point of failure wearing a badge.

Educate the room the same way you educate the agent. Show managers what a blast-radius answer looks like. Show developers where the map lives and when it goes stale. Shared context is not a slide. It is the index everyone agrees to query before they trust speed.

Then I change what humans review.

review the blast-radius list before first ship
review which flows the change touches
review whether the map was refreshed after the last commit
do not review only the open file the agent rewrote

Control is still what is allowed to ship. A tidy diff on an open file is not permission. Permission is a change whose callers you can name, whose flows you can test, and whose owner can still refuse the merge when the radius is unknown.

I am not arguing against agents. I am arguing against blind ones. Give them a map. Make them ask for the radius before they edit. Keep the map honest. Put the proof outside the model.

That is how you keep ten-times speed without trading away the boring craft that made the system survivable in the first place.

Ask for the blast radius before the edit. Then decide whether the change is allowed to ship.

medium.titulo: Choose a Claude integration by who owns the work after the prompt
medium.resumo: Imagine a team preparing release notes for version 2.4.
medium.conteudo_html:
Imagine a team preparing release notes for version 2.4. The draft must use approved changes, link each claim to its source and flag missing evidence. One ticket says a bug is fixed, but the release branch contains no matching change. The task is to produce a reviewable draft, not publish it. Which Claude integration fits this workflow?

This article was generated with AI assistance. I am building Cred Farmer, an independent Claude certification preparation platform, and this is a practical adaptation of its guide. Cred Farmer is not affiliated with Anthropic or Pearson VUE. The release-note scenario is fictional, not a reported project outcome.

Start by assigning responsibility for gathering evidence, running tools, handling failures and accepting the draft. Claude Code, the Agent SDK and direct API integration offer different ways to organize that work. They are not a simple ladder on which each step removes the same responsibilities.

First decide where the workflow belongs

An engineer working in a repository could use Claude Code from the terminal to inspect relevant changes and prepare a draft. The engineer still chooses the release boundaries and reviews the output. This can be a reasonable starting point when the task belongs in an existing development workflow.

The CLI is not limited to interactive use. The official integration comparison also describes running it as a subprocess with the -p flag and JSON output. Headless execution changes how a surrounding system invokes the work; it does not settle who handles credentials, approvals, failures or the resulting artifact.

If the same workflow must live inside a Python or TypeScript application, the Agent SDK offers programmatic access to the Claude Code agent. It supplies the loop and capabilities such as tools, sessions and permissions. Your application operates that process and must decide how its results become a usable release-note draft.

Hosting is another decision. The comparison lists Managed Agents separately: Anthropic runs the agent harness, with an Anthropic-managed or self-hosted sandbox. That is distinct from embedding the Agent SDK in a process you operate. None of these descriptions establishes that one option is best for every release workflow.

Direct API access does not always mean writing every loop

Suppose the application already has approved-change and release-branch services. It needs Claude to call those narrow operations and return a draft in an application-defined format. A Client SDK could fit that design without adopting the broader Claude Code environment.

A manual tool loop gives the application responsibility for sending requests, executing requested tools and returning their results. However, the Client SDK tool runner can handle the request cycle, tool execution and conversation state. It is currently documented as beta. Direct API access therefore does not imply that every caller must implement this machinery from scratch.

Choose based on the control required. The tool-runner documentation recommends a manual loop for human approval, custom logging or conditional execution. It also exposes ways to inspect responses and take over message history. If you take over that history, you must preserve a valid conversation and a termination path; convenience does not remove those obligations.

Write down what a successful draft must prove

For the fictional release, define an evidence contract before choosing a surface. Each proposed release-note claim should name its approved ticket and matching release change. A claim with missing or conflicting support should appear as an unresolved question, not a confident sentence in the publishable draft.

Separate execution success from acceptance. The Agent SDK loop documentation describes final results and errors for turn or budget limits. A completed agent response is evidence that the loop ended, not proof that the release notes satisfy the contract. The application or reviewer still checks the artifact against the source records.

Keep publishing outside the drafting process and give it a separate authorized review step. Also distinguish available tools from automatic approval: the SDK’s allowedTools setting auto-approves listed tools; omitted tools can remain available and follow other permission rules. A short approval list alone does not establish an exclusive capability boundary.

Assign the failure path before an unattended run

Decide what happens if the approved-change service times out, a tool is denied or the run exhausts its limit. Save the draft as incomplete when evidence is missing, record which inputs were checked and retain enough execution detail to diagnose the gap. These are proposed application requirements, not results from a tested implementation.

An unattended job also needs an owner for interrupted runs and duplicate work. Before retrying, check whether a draft was already saved. If later versions add publication, verify that operation’s state before repeating it. A loop supplied by a library does not establish whether an external action is safe to retry.

Try the decision on one page

Sketch three versions: an engineer using the CLI, an application embedding the Agent SDK and an application using a Client SDK. For each, name the process operator, tool-execution owner, approval route, failure handler and artifact reviewer. Then introduce the missing release-branch change. Where is it detected, and who prevents the unsupported claim from reaching publication?

Choose the version whose responsibilities fit the real system, and test those boundaries before expanding the workflow. For the source discussion behind this exercise, see the Cred Farmer guide to the Agent SDK, Claude Code and the API.

medium.titulo: Small Language Models: Why 2026 Became the Year Bigger Stopped Meaning Better
medium.resumo: For three straight years, the story of AI progress was simple: more parameters, more compute, more capability. GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini…
medium.conteudo_html:
For three straight years, the story of AI progress was simple: more parameters, more compute, more capability. GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini captured headlines by getting bigger. Somewhere in the middle of that race, a quieter story started developing at the opposite end of the spectrum — and by 2026, it had become impossible to ignore.

Microsoft’s Phi-3.5-Mini, a model with roughly 3.8 billion parameters, started matching the performance of models forty times its size on a range of benchmarks. Google’s Gemma runs entirely on a smartphone. Alibaba’s Qwen2 fits on hardware as small as a smartwatch and still handles genuinely complex reasoning. None of these needed a data center. Small language models — SLMs — had quietly become good enough to matter.

What Actually Changed

The distinction is mostly about scale and where the model runs. Frontier LLMs sit in the 70-billion-to-trillion-plus parameter range and typically require cloud-hosted GPU clusters to serve. SLMs, by contrast, generally run somewhere between 1 and 13 billion parameters — small enough to fit on a phone, laptop, or embedded device without an internet connection.

What made 2026 the turning point wasn’t just that small models existed — they always had — it’s that they stopped being a compromise. Multiple industry benchmarks now show SLMs delivering around 90% of a frontier model’s practical capability at roughly 10% of the cost. Serving a 7-billion-parameter model can be 10 to 30 times cheaper than serving a 70-to-175-billion-parameter one for the same task, and that cost gap compounds fast at real usage volume.

Three engineering shifts made this possible: dedicated Neural Processing Units now shipping in most modern phone chipsets, hybrid architectures that blend state-space models with traditional attention for higher throughput, and aggressive quantization techniques — including 1.58-bit “BitNet” models that represent weights using only three values instead of the usual 32-bit floating point range.

Why Enterprises Started Caring

Cost was the first reason companies took notice, but it stopped being the only one. Gartner’s 2025 AI Infrastructure Report found that enterprise spending on locally-run models increased 40% year-over-year — and cost wasn’t the primary driver cited. Two other factors mattered just as much:

Data residency. Running a model on-device or on-premises means sensitive data never has to leave the building, which matters enormously for regulated industries — finance, healthcare, legal — where sending customer or patient data to a third-party cloud API creates real compliance exposure.

Latency. Cloud-hosted LLMs typically introduce 500 milliseconds to 2 seconds of delay per request. For anything interactive — a voice assistant, a live customer support widget, an in-app copilot — that lag is noticeable and often unacceptable. SLMs running on NPU hardware routinely respond in under 100 milliseconds, and some benchmarks report edge latency as low as 32 milliseconds on mobile-class chips.

Where Small Models Are Already Doing Real Work

Adoption isn’t hypothetical anymore. Small models are already handling:

  • Document processing and classification — sorting, tagging, and extracting structured data from high volumes of routine documents.
  • Code generation and debugging — working alongside developers on well-scoped, narrow coding tasks rather than open-ended architecture decisions.
  • On-device assistants — voice and text interactions that need to work offline or respond instantly.
  • Regulated-industry copilots — finance, legal, and medical tools where compliance requirements make cloud processing a liability rather than a convenience.
  • The bulk of agentic loops — parsing an input, calling a tool, formatting a structured result, repeating.

That last one has turned out to be the biggest shift. NVIDIA’s own research has made the case that small models, not frontier ones, are the right default for most steps inside an AI agent’s workflow.

The Bigger Claim: Frontier Capability and Everyday Value Have Split Apart

The argument researchers are making now goes beyond “small models save money.” It’s that the smartest available model is rarely the one a given task actually needs. Most steps inside an agentic workflow — parsing text, calling a known tool, formatting output — don’t require frontier-level reasoning at all; they require speed, consistency, and low cost, repeated thousands of times.

That’s producing a specific architectural pattern across the industry: an SLM-first router. A small, fast, local model handles the large majority of steps in a task — commonly cited around 80 to 90% — and only escalates to a frontier cloud model when it hits something genuinely difficult or open-ended. The deciding question shifts from “which model is smartest” to “which model is cheap and private enough to run this specific loop at the scale I actually need.”

Gartner has projected that by 2027, organizations will use small, task-specific models roughly three times more than general-purpose LLMs. That’s not a prediction that big models disappear — it’s a prediction about division of labor.

What SLMs Still Can’t Do

None of this makes frontier LLMs obsolete, and the more careful voices in this field are explicit about that. Small models sacrifice generality for efficiency — they’re built to be very good at a narrower set of tasks, not to match a frontier model’s breadth of open-ended reasoning. A few real limitations to keep in mind:

  • Where “small” is too small. Below a certain parameter count, models start failing on tasks with genuine ambiguity or multi-step novel reasoning — the exact cases that still belong on a frontier model.
  • Fine-tuning still takes real work. Getting an SLM to match frontier-quality output on a specific domain usually requires deliberate fine-tuning, not just picking a smaller model off the shelf.
  • Routing logic adds complexity. Building a reliable system that knows when to escalate from a small model to a large one is itself a nontrivial engineering problem — one that has to be tuned per workload rather than assumed from a vendor’s headline benchmark.
  • Benchmarks vary by task. A model that performs well on general knowledge tests may still underperform on a company’s specific, narrow use case — practitioners increasingly recommend benchmarking a candidate model on your own data before committing to it.

The practical takeaway for 2026 isn’t “switch everything to small models.” It’s closer to what one industry researcher put it plainly: stop paying jet fares to deliver letters. Match the model to the job — and for a large share of everyday AI work, that job has turned out to be smaller than the industry originally assumed.

Sources: Zylos Research, “Small Language Models and Edge AI: The 2026 Shift to Local Intelligence,” February 2026; InfoWorld, “Small language models: Rethinking enterprise AI architecture,” May 2026; Digital Applied, “Small Language Models for On-Device Agents in 2026,” June 2026; Knolli, “Small Language Models: A Complete Guide for 2026.” This article reflects publicly available information as of September 2026.

medium.titulo: I built a Vue directive that turns your real component into its own skeleton
medium.resumo: Skeleton loaders have a maintenance problem. You build a second version of every component by hand: a grey circle where the avatar goes…
medium.conteudo_html:
Skeleton loaders have a maintenance problem. You build a second version of every component by hand: a grey circle where the avatar goes, three bars where the text goes. Then someone adds a badge to the real card, and the skeleton quietly stops matching.

I wanted the skeleton to come from the component itself. So I built v-skeleton, a directive in vue-smart-loading-kit:

While loading is true, every line of text becomes a bar, images and buttons become solid blocks, and borders and spacing stay exactly as they are. When loading ends, the real content is back. Try it in the live demo (Skeletonize page, tick "loading").

This post is about how it works, and about the bugs that only showed up because of how I tested it.

The rule: never change the DOM

The obvious approach is to measure the real elements and render placeholder boxes over them. That needs JavaScript on every render, and every resize, and it fights with your layout.

I took the opposite route. The directive only toggles a class, a few CSS variables and two attributes on the element:

Everything else is CSS. No element is added, removed or resized, so nothing can move. That turned out to be the most important design decision, and the hardest to keep.

Hiding text without breaking borders

My first version hid text with color: transparent. It looked right until a code review found that it also erased every border, divider and icon that uses currentColor. A card with a 1px solid currentColor border lost its border.

The fix is a property most people never touch:

text-fill-color paints only the glyphs. color, and everything that inherits it through currentColor, keeps its real value.

One bar per line of text

To draw bars where the lines are, I mask the element’s background with a repeating gradient sized by the lh unit (one line-height):

Each line gets a bar, with a gap between lines. A paragraph that wraps to three lines gets three bars, at whatever width the browser chose.

Masking the whole element has a side effect: it also hides the element’s own border, which matters for table cells. So the mask has two more layers, a border-box layer and a padding-box layer combined with mask-composite: exclude. Together they leave a ring where the border is, so table grid lines survive.

Images get object-position: -99999px, which slides the picture out of its own box while the box keeps its size and radius. Buttons and inputs become solid blocks.

Proving that nothing moves

“Nothing moves” is easy to claim and hard to test. jsdom, which most Vue tests run in, has no layout engine: every element is 0×0, so any position assertion passes.

So the visual rules are tested in a real Chromium with Vitest Browser Mode and Playwright. The main test records the bounding box of every element, turns the skeleton on, and records them again:

It runs in CI on every push, so any CSS change that shifts a single pixel fails the build.

The SSR bug I almost shipped

With server rendering and placeholder data, you want the skeleton in the server HTML, so fake content never flashes. Directives don’t run on the server, but Vue has a getSSRProps hook for exactly this, and Vue 3.5's data-allow-mismatch lets hydration accept the attributes the client sets again.

The bug was in restoring attributes. When the skeleton ends, the directive puts back whatever inert and aria-hidden the element had before. My first version read "before" from the DOM. After SSR, the DOM already contained the skeleton's own inert, so it saved inert as the original value. When loading ended, it restored it, and the whole section stayed unclickable forever.

The fix was to read the original values from the vnode, which is what the template actually binds, never from the DOM. A test now server-renders, hydrates, ends the load and checks that no attribute is left behind.

Timing: when to show it at all

A skeleton that flashes for 80ms on a fast request feels worse than no skeleton. So v-skeleton waits 200ms before showing anything, and once shown it stays for at least 500ms so it never blinks off:

The timing tests use fake timers and record the value at every 10ms step, so a single wrong frame fails them. Checking only the final state would miss a flash in the middle.

What 100% coverage missed

The package had about 99% line coverage, and I still didn’t know whether the tests would notice a broken default. So I ran Stryker, which plants small bugs in the source (flips a condition, changes a constant, drops a call) and reruns the tests for each one.

The first score was 80%. Some of the surviving mutants were real gaps: you could change the table skeleton’s default row height and no test failed. Two were real bugs:

  • v-skeleton removed an aria-hidden that the template had bound to false, while Vue itself renders it as "false".
  • The color helper accepted #12345z as a valid hex color, because parseInt("5z", 16) stops at the bad digit and returns 5.

After closing the gaps the score is above 90%. The rest are mostly equivalent mutants, changes no test could observe, which is why 100% isn’t the goal.

Limits

It’s CSS, so it has CSS’s blind spots. The last line of a wrapped paragraph gets a full-width bar, because CSS can’t know where the text ends. A few characters on a colored circle (an initials avatar) look like text, so you mark them data-skeleton="block". And it needs browsers from late 2023 on, for :has(), lh and mask-composite.

Try it

npm install vue-smart-loading-kit

The kit also has a SmartLoader component with an error state and retry, 13 skeleton variants, 9 spinners and progress bars.

I’d love feedback, especially on layouts where the skeleton doesn’t look right.

Originally published at https://dev.to on October 3, 2026.

medium.titulo: SaaS Laravel — A Laravel Starter Kit for Building SaaS Products Faster
medium.resumo: SaaS Laravel: Stop Rebuilding the Same SaaS Features Every Time. Starting a new SaaS product is exciting.
medium.conteudo_html:
SaaS Laravel: Stop Rebuilding the Same SaaS Features Every Time. Starting a new SaaS product is exciting.

You have an idea, you know what you want to build, and you want to start working on the part that actually makes your product different.

Then reality hits.

Before you can work on the real product, you end up building the same things again:

  • Authentication
  • User profiles
  • Teams
  • Permissions
  • Invitations
  • Notifications
  • Settings
  • Activity logs
  • Dashboard layouts
  • Account management
  • Frontend components
  • Error states
  • Email flows

None of these features are unusual.

But almost every SaaS application needs them.

And rebuilding them for every new project takes a lot of time.

That is why I built SaaS Laravel.

Website: https://saas-laravel.com/

What Is SaaS Laravel?

SaaS Laravel is a set of Laravel starter kits built for developers who want a solid starting point for a SaaS application.

The idea is simple:

Start with the common SaaS work already organized, then spend your time building your actual product.

It is not a no-code platform.

It is not a closed system.

And it is not trying to hide Laravel from you.

You still work with your Laravel application normally. You own the code, you can change it, extend it, remove parts you do not need, or build completely new features on top of it.

SaaS Laravel simply gives you a better place to start.

Why I Built It

Whenever I started a new SaaS project, I noticed the same pattern.

I would spend the first few days or weeks rebuilding things I had already built before.

Create authentication.

Create the dashboard.

Add user settings.

Add team members.

Create invitations.

Add permissions.

Create notifications.

Build common frontend components.

Handle empty states.

Add profile pages.

Set up project structure.

And only after all of that could I start working on the feature that actually made the product interesting.

That felt wasteful.

So instead of rebuilding the same foundation for every project, I wanted one clean base that I could reuse.

That became SaaS Laravel.

Start With the Essentials Already in Place

A starter kit should save time without making the code difficult to understand.

That is why SaaS Laravel focuses on features that most SaaS products need sooner or later.

You start with a working foundation and then shape it around your product.

Some of the common pieces include:

  • Authentication
  • User accounts
  • Teams
  • Member management
  • Permissions
  • Invitations
  • Notifications
  • Settings
  • Activity-related features
  • Reusable UI
  • Common layouts
  • Developer-friendly project structure

Instead of starting from an empty project, you start from something that already feels like an application.

Authentication Is Already Part of the Foundation

Authentication is usually one of the first things we build.

Login.

Registration.

Password reset.

Email verification.

Account-related pages.

It is necessary, but it is rarely the reason someone is building a SaaS product.

SaaS Laravel gives you a working authenticated application so you can move on to more important product work.

You can still customize the flow whenever your application needs something different.

Teams Without Building Everything From Scratch

A lot of SaaS products eventually become multi-user products.

One person creates an account.

Then they want to invite a teammate.

Then another.

Soon you need:

  • Team members
  • Invitations
  • Access control
  • Member management
  • Different permissions

This can quickly become a project of its own.

SaaS Laravel gives this part a clear structure from the beginning.

Instead of figuring out the entire team system while building your actual product, you already have a foundation you can extend.

Simple Permission Management

Not every user should be able to do everything.

An owner may have full access.

Another user may only be able to view data.

Someone else may be able to create records but not delete them.

These rules become important very quickly in real SaaS products.

SaaS Laravel includes a straightforward permission approach so your application can control access without turning permission management into unnecessary complexity.

The important part is that you can adapt it to your own product rules.

Invitations That Feel Like Part of the Product

Inviting someone sounds like a small feature.

But once you build it properly, you need to think about:

  • Who can invite users?
  • What happens if the email is already registered?
  • What happens if it is not?
  • When does an invitation expire?
  • Can it be resent?
  • Can it be cancelled?
  • What access should the invited person receive?

These are small decisions individually, but together they take time.

A starter kit should give you a sensible starting point instead of making you solve the same problem again.

Notifications Without Reinventing the UI

Notifications appear in almost every modern application.

A team member joins.

Something is updated.

A task completes.

An invitation arrives.

An important action needs the user’s attention.

Creating the backend event is only one part of the job.

You also need a usable interface for displaying notifications and handling read/unread states.

SaaS Laravel provides a foundation for this so notifications can feel like a normal part of your application instead of another standalone feature you need to design from zero.

Settings Should Be Easy to Extend

Every application eventually grows a settings area.

At first, maybe it is only the user’s name and email.

Later you may need:

  • Account settings
  • Team settings
  • Application preferences
  • Notification preferences
  • Security settings
  • Product-specific configuration

SaaS Laravel gives settings a clear home in the application.

You can keep adding your own options without turning the settings area into an unorganized collection of pages.

A UI You Can Actually Change

A starter kit should not force you to keep its design forever.

Your product will have its own brand.

Its own colors.

Its own layout decisions.

Its own components.

That is expected.

The purpose of the included UI is to save you from beginning with a blank page.

Use it as it is when it works for you.

Change it when it does not.

The code is yours.

Choose Your Frontend

Different developers prefer different frontend frameworks.

Some prefer Vue.

Some work faster in React.

Others enjoy Svelte.

SaaS Laravel is designed around that reality.

You can choose the frontend you are comfortable with instead of changing your entire development workflow just because a starter kit picked one framework.

The available starter-kit options include:

  • Vue
  • React
  • Svelte

The important part is that they share the same Laravel foundation.

One Laravel Foundation, Multiple Frontend Choices

Maintaining separate Laravel applications for Vue, React, and Svelte would create unnecessary duplication.

Fix something in one project and you would have to repeat the same change in the others.

That is exactly what I wanted to avoid.

The goal of SaaS Laravel is to keep the common backend foundation consistent while allowing different frontend implementations.

Conceptually:

Laravel
                │
        Shared SaaS Core
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────┐
      │         │         │
     Vue      React     Svelte

The business foundation stays familiar.

You choose how you want to render the product.

Use It As-Is or Make It Yours

SaaS Laravel is not intended to be a rigid template.

Think of it as a starting point.

Maybe you need everything it provides.

Maybe you only need half of it.

That is fine.

You can:

  • Remove features
  • Rename things
  • Change layouts
  • Replace components
  • Add your own modules
  • Change the data model
  • Build your own business logic
  • Customize the frontend completely

A starter kit should make your first steps faster, not decide what your final product must look like.

Built for Real Development

A polished screenshot is nice.

But developers eventually have to work with the code.

That is why project structure matters.

When a project grows, you need to know where things belong.

You should be able to open the application a few months later and still understand how it is organized.

SaaS Laravel aims to keep the structure predictable so adding new features does not slowly turn the project into something difficult to maintain.

Common Components Save More Time Than You Think

Buttons, inputs, selects, checkboxes, labels and validation messages seem small.

But when every page creates its own version, inconsistency starts to appear quickly.

One button looks different.

Another input handles errors differently.

One page uses a different spacing system.

A reusable component layer helps keep those small details consistent.

That means when you improve one common component, many parts of the application improve with it.

Built With Customization in Mind

There is a big difference between a starter kit and a finished SaaS product.

Your product will still need its own:

  • Database design
  • Business rules
  • Workflows
  • Features
  • Branding
  • Integrations
  • Emails
  • Pricing
  • Product experience

And that is exactly where your development time should go.

The starter kit handles the common foundation.

You build the part people are actually paying for.

Developer Experience Matters

A good starter kit should reduce friction.

You should not spend hours trying to understand why something was built in an unusual way.

The code should feel familiar to someone already comfortable with Laravel.

That is also why I prefer keeping the product close to normal Laravel development rather than hiding everything behind proprietary abstractions.

You are still building a Laravel application.

You simply begin further ahead.

AI Coding Tools Work Better With Consistent Structure

AI coding assistants are becoming part of normal development workflows.

But they work much better when a project has clear patterns.

If one feature uses one folder structure and the next feature uses a completely different approach, generated code can quickly become inconsistent.

A predictable starter-kit structure gives both developers and coding agents a clearer pattern to follow.

For example, instead of asking an AI agent to invent an entire user-management architecture, you can ask it to extend the existing structure.

That usually produces cleaner results and requires less cleanup afterwards.

You Still Own the Code

This is important.

SaaS Laravel is meant to help developers build their own products.

It should not turn your application into something you cannot control.

You get the code.

You work with it directly.

You can understand it.

And you can change it.

There is no reason your SaaS product should become dependent on a visual builder or proprietary runtime just because you wanted to save some development time at the beginning.

Who Is SaaS Laravel For?

SaaS Laravel can be useful if you are:

  • Building your first SaaS
  • Launching another SaaS product
  • Creating an internal business tool
  • Building a client SaaS application
  • Prototyping a product
  • Creating a micro-SaaS
  • Working alone
  • Working with a small team

It is especially useful if you already know Laravel and want to spend less time rebuilding common application infrastructure.

Who Probably Does Not Need It?

Not every project needs a starter kit.

If you are building a very small application with only one or two pages, starting with a fresh Laravel installation may be perfectly fine.

And if your project has an extremely unusual architecture, you may prefer building everything yourself.

SaaS Laravel is most useful when your project looks like a typical modern SaaS application and you would otherwise spend time recreating the same common features.

The Goal Is Simple: Ship Faster

The goal is not to generate an entire SaaS business for you.

The goal is to remove unnecessary repetition.

Instead of this:

New idea
   ↓
Build authentication
   ↓
Build dashboard
   ↓
Build teams
   ↓
Build permissions
   ↓
Build invitations
   ↓
Build notifications
   ↓
Build settings
   ↓
Finally start the product

You can get closer to this:

New idea
   ↓
Start with SaaS Laravel
   ↓
Customize the foundation
   ↓
Build your actual product

That is the difference I wanted from a starter kit.

One-Time Access

I also wanted the purchasing model to stay simple.

Instead of another recurring development subscription, the starter kits are offered with one-time access.

Choose the framework you actually use, or get access to the complete set if you work across multiple frontend stacks.

The current options and details are available directly on the website.

View the starter kits:
https://saas-laravel.com/

Start With a Better Foundation

Building a SaaS product is already difficult.

There are plenty of real problems to solve:

Finding customers.

Building something useful.

Improving onboarding.

Listening to feedback.

Fixing bugs.

Shipping new features.

You probably do not need to add “build another settings screen from scratch” to that list.

That is what SaaS Laravel is for.

A clean starting point.

Common SaaS features already organized.

Laravel code you can actually work with.

And the freedom to turn it into your own product.

If you are starting a Laravel SaaS and want to spend more time on the product instead of rebuilding the foundation, take a look:

SaaS Laravel
https://saas-laravel.com/

corrida_no_ar.titulo: CONHEÇA o ZYLA: Treino de CORRIDA com INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Conheça a Zyla em uma entrevista com o cofundador Guilherme Monteiro. Saiba como o app brasileiro usa IA e a metodologia de Jack Daniels para criar treinos personalizados, sua integração com relógios GPS, planos de expansão internacional e os valores dos planos de assinatura.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Domingo | 4 de outubro de 2026

Você já ouviu falar da Zyla? É um aplicativo brasileiro que oferece treinamentos de corrida unindo metodologia e inteligência artificial. Durante o TS Summit, bati um papo com Guilherme Monteiro, um dos fundadores da plataforma, para entender os bastidores, a tecnologia por trás dos treinos e os planos para o futuro. A Zyla, inclusive, foi anunciada recentemente como o aplicativo oficial de treinamento da Corrida de São Silvestre.

A conversa começou de forma descontraída, com Guilherme revelando a origem do nome “Zyla”: ele pediu ao ChatGPT por palavras de quatro letras sem significado em nenhuma língua, e Zyla estava na lista. O aplicativo é uma plataforma de treinamento de corrida que combina uma metodologia consolidada com inteligência artificial para gerar treinos personalizados.

Dos treinos com ChatGPT à criação do app

A ideia para a Zyla surgiu de uma experiência pessoal de Guilherme. Antes de procurar uma assessoria, ele tentou treinar usando o ChatGPT. Sendo “extremamente confiante”, ele pedia treinos intensos, como correr 7 vezes por semana com longos de 35 km por cinco semanas seguidas para uma maratona. O resultado? Uma fratura por estresse. Essa lesão o fez perceber que, embora a personalização da IA fosse interessante, faltava a metodologia e o profissionalismo de um guia. Assim nasceu a Zyla, com o objetivo de unir o melhor dos dois mundos e democratizar o acesso a treinos personalizados. Atualmente, o aplicativo já ultrapassou a marca de 130 mil atletas, com mais de 60 mil treinando ativamente para alguma prova.

Crescimento e estratégias de aquisição

Um dos principais canais de crescimento da Zyla foi a integração com o Wellhub (antigo Gympass). A plataforma se tornou uma solução para os usuários que queriam treinar corrida, mas enfrentavam a dificuldade de precisar fazer o check-in em um ponto físico de uma assessoria, o que consumia o crédito diário que poderia ser usado na academia. Além disso, a Zyla trabalha fortemente com “running clubs” e criadores de conteúdo, que funcionam como importantes canais de distribuição e engajamento.

Como os treinos são montados?

Ao baixar o aplicativo, o usuário preenche uma anamnese detalhada para que a plataforma o conheça melhor. A partir daí, o sistema aplica limitações para garantir a segurança do corredor. Por exemplo, um iniciante que queira treinar sete dias por semana será orientado a começar com três. O app utiliza a metodologia clássica de Jack Daniels, calculando o VDOT do atleta com base em uma pergunta curiosa para estimar o tempo nos 5 km: “Se um leão estivesse atrás de você amanhã, em quanto tempo você correria 5 km na sua velocidade máxima?”.

Integração com relógios e futuro GPS próprio

A Zyla possui conexão direta com os principais relógios do mercado, como Garmin, Apple Watch e Amazfit, permitindo o envio de treinos estruturados em duas vias (leitura e escrita). A integração com a Coros será lançada na próxima semana. No entanto, algumas marcas como Samsung e Polar ainda não permitem o envio de treinos, apenas a leitura dos dados. Pensando nos 70% de usuários que não possuem relógio, o aplicativo está desenvolvendo seu próprio GPS nativo, eliminando a dependência do Strava para o registro das atividades.

Distâncias, planos de expansão e visão de produto

Atualmente, a Zyla oferece planos de treino para distâncias que vão de 5 km até a maratona, com a possibilidade de customizar percursos intermediários, como a prova de 8 km do Ayrton Senna. A plataforma não tem planos de incluir ultramaratonas. A internacionalização está no radar, com a tradução para inglês e espanhol prevista para o primeiro trimestre do próximo ano, impulsionada pelo crescimento do Wellhub nos EUA. A visão da Zyla é atuar como um “ótimo coadjuvante” no universo da corrida, fornecendo software para quem está na rua, como eventos e “running clubs”. Em breve, será lançado um módulo de clubes, onde cada grupo terá seu próprio sticker personalizado para compartilhar nos treinos.

Quanto custa?

A Zyla oferece um plano mensal por R$ 39,90, um semestral por R$ 139,90 e um anual por R$ 229,90. Para quem é usuário do Wellhub a partir do plano “Basic”, o acesso ao aplicativo é gratuito e não consome o check-in diário.
